46x7gm: With «haber» you report an action that was done and the participle never changes: «hemos revisado las fichas». With «tener», «llevar» and «dejar» you present the result of that action, and then the participle behaves like an adjective of the direct object: it agrees with it in gender and number. «Tengo revisadas las fichas», «llevamos embaladas doscientas cajas», «dejé cerrada la bodega».
11rb79g: Each verb adds a nuance. «Tener» presents something ready, available. «Llevar» adds up what has been done so far and leaves the task open, so it usually comes with a quantity. «Dejar» tells how something was left when you went away or let go of it. There are also fixed forms that don't agree because they have no visible object: «tengo entendido que…», «tengo pensado mudarme», «te tengo dicho que no…».

1claxd2: With «quedar» and «quedarse» the participle agrees with the subject. «Quedar» is used mainly with things and situations, often without anyone wanting it: «la puerta quedó abierta toda la noche». «Quedarse» appears more with people and usually expresses something involuntary: «me quedé dormida en el bus». «Ir» and «andar» describe how someone or something is while moving or during a phase: «el seguro va incluido», «anda preocupado desde el lunes».
15lud6b: Some verbs have two participles. With «haber» both are valid («han imprimido» and «han impreso», «ha freído» and «ha frito»), but as an adjective the irregular one is preferred: «los folletos impresos». Other adjectives look like participles but aren't: you say «estoy despierto» but «me he despertado». And several participles gained a new meaning as adjectives: a «leída» person has read a lot, an «atrevida» person takes risks and someone «agradecido» feels grateful.

1itz1iu: Obligation or deduction: deber, deber de and tener que
gritn2: «Deber + infinitive» expresses an obligation or firm advice: «debes devolver el libro el viernes». «Deber de + infinitive» expresses a deduction: you don't know something for sure, but you assume it from what you see. «Debe de ser el camión: ya son las nueve». Grammars also accept «deber» without «de» for deducing, but advise against using «deber de» to oblige.
blnngu: Deduction can look at the past: «debía de ser muy tarde», «debió de olvidarse», «debe de haber llovido toda la noche». When the deduction is almost certain, «tener que» is used: «tiene que haber una gotera en el techo, el suelo está mojado». That way you can rank how sure you are: «tiene que» (almost certain), «debe de» (probable), «a lo mejor» or «quizás» (possible).
njb7yj: Ask yourself whether someone is giving an order or making an assumption. If it's an assumption, add «de» and the sentence becomes clear to any reader.

rug3z9: «Haber de + infinitive» is an obligation typical of formal or written texts: «los libros han de devolverse en buen estado». In Mexican speech and in other areas it is also used to make assumptions: «ha de estar en la oficina». «Haber que» is impersonal and is conjugated in every tense, always in the singular: «hubo que», «había que», «habrá que», «habría que», «aunque haya que». «Debe de haber» is also singular when «haber» means to exist: «debe de haber cien cajas», never «deben de haber».
1j4k7il: «Venir a + infinitive» is used to approximate a figure («la mudanza viene a costar trescientos mil pesos») or to sum up an equivalence («lo que propone viene a ser cerrar un mes»). And if you want to soften an obligation, put the verb in the conditional: «deberías», «tendrías que», «habría que».

1tn0dq3: Entry from a community library's newsletter
rrfhrl: Original SpanishCue text written as the newsletter of the fictional Rayen library in Temuco. The people and places are invented.
1ur8770: For twelve years, the Rayen Library operated in the neighbourhood parish hall. When the parish told us it needed the space, many of us thought we would have to close. That didn't happen: the neighbourhood council offered us a wooden house three blocks away, with a courtyard and a large room that used to be a sewing workshop. The contract was signed in September and we haven't stopped since.
19r8182: Today we can take stock for the first time. We have almost four thousand books inventoried and three hundred boxes packed so far, each one labelled by section. The metal shelves are dismantled in the hallway, and the wooden ones, which were too heavy, we left installed in the parish as a donation for catechism classes. The volunteers from the carpentry workshop plan to build new furniture from salvaged boards.
1yloof0: Not everything has gone well. In the first week we found a damp patch in the kitchen of the new house. For days we argued about the cause: some said there had to be a leak; others, that the neighbour must be watering against the wall. In the end a builder climbed onto the roof and found a loose zinc sheet. It had to be replaced before we brought in the books, because wet paper can't be saved. The repair came to about the same as two months of electricity.
1jlbgpp: We also learned something about ourselves. A project like this must have clear rules, but it can't depend on just one person. That's why every Saturday someone writes on the whiteboard which boxes were moved and what's missing. Nobody should take keys home, and every night the last person to leave turns off the heaters. It seems obvious, but one Friday the courtyard door was left open and a dog came in and fell asleep on the children's section.
xqgq7y: If all goes well, we will open the new house on the first Saturday of December. We'll have to paint the front and finish the shelves, and there must still be about a hundred boxes at the parish. If you have a free afternoon, come along: you don't need to know about books, just bring some enthusiasm and, if you can, a flask of tea.
